title: Are two ways of breaking sixty three into primes different?
description: Sixty three is broken into primes in two ways, giving three times three times seven and three times seven times three. The board counts the threes and the sevens in each way, then Keeko doubts that a new order makes a new answer.
teaching_notes: One idea: the same primes occur the same number of times in every way of breaking a number, and only the order changes. Watch for students who think a new order gives a different prime factorisation.

source: By going through different ways of breaking down the number,
video_script.why: The child sees that two ways of breaking sixty three into primes use the same primes the same number of times.
video_script.substitution: the book's own number, sixty three, broken into primes in two ways
video_script.anchor: the number sixty three broken into primes in two ways
video_script.wrong_answer: they are different, because the numbers come in a different order
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko sees the primes in a different order and calls the two prime factorisations different.
video_script.payoff_line: Not really, because the same primes occur the same number of times

final_answer.value: Not really: the same primes 3 and 7 occur in both, 3 two times and 7 once
final_answer.spoken: Not really, because the same primes occur the same number of times

maths_rules: in both ways 3 occurs two times and 7 occurs once
the two ways differ only in order
video_script.design: The two ways of breaking sixty three stand side by side in two colours. Each prime is counted in each way, and the counts match.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about breaking sixty three into prime numbers.
<bookmark mark='first'/>One way gives three times three times seven.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Another way gives three times seven times three.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Are the two ways different?

beats.on_screen: the two ways stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the words prime factorisation; 63 is split as 9 × 7 and again as 3 × 21 with the factors still to be broken

marks.term: the words prime factorisation appear with the meaning a product of primes
marks.split: 63 splits as 9 × 7 and as 3 × 21, and 9 and 21 are marked as not yet prime

narration: <bookmark mark='term'/>Writing a number as a product of primes is called its prime factorisation.
<bookmark mark='split'/>Sixty three splits as nine times seven, and also as three times twenty one. Nine and twenty one must break further.

beats.on_screen: Given: 63 = 3 × 3 × 7 and 63 = 3 × 7 × 3, two ways of breaking 63 into primes

marks.given: the two ways are written under the word Given

beats.colours: first way in teal, second way in amber
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, two ways of breaking sixty three into primes.

beats.on_screen: To find: are the two ways different?
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find if the two ways of breaking sixty three are really different.
<bookmark mark='nine'/>Step one, take the first way. Sixty three is nine times seven, and nine is three times three.
<bookmark mark='way'/>Putting the primes together gives three times three times seven.
<bookmark mark='twenty'/>Step two, take the second way. Sixty three is three times twenty one, and twenty one is seven times three.
<bookmark mark='way'/>Putting the primes together gives three times seven times three.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: count the primes: in 3 × 3 × 7 the prime 3 occurs two times and 7 once; in 3 × 7 × 3 the prime 3 occurs two times and 7 once

marks.count: the primes of the first way are counted, and 3 shows two, 7 shows one
marks.same: the primes of the second way are counted, and the same counts appear

beats.colours: threes in teal, sevens in amber
narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step three, count each prime in the first way. Three occurs two times and seven occurs once.
<bookmark mark='same'/>Count again in the second way. Three occurs two times and seven occurs once.

beats.on_screen: Answer: Not really: the same primes 3 and 7 occur in both, 3 two times and 7 once

marks.ans: the answer is boxed in green

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Not really, because the same primes occur the same number of times. The only thing that changes between the two ways is the order.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the board
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble says the ways are different because of the order; the primes of the two ways are joined by lines; the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

marks.join: lines join each prime of the first way to the same prime in the second way

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks they are different, because the numbers come in a different order.
<bookmark mark='join'/>But each prime in the first way has a partner in the second way. Nothing is left over.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>A new order of the same primes is not a new prime factorisation.
